transcript: Chapter 35. Kiva. One door each. Kellan was at the draft board at eight, in the black and gold, reading his own card with his hands in his pockets. Kiva saw him from across the boards and went over. She had meant to find him at the loft and had missed him. He had gone down the stair at six, Prue said, before anybody else was dressed, with his boots in his hand, so as not to wake the room. Now he stood alone in front of the deal board, with the green bays along its top, and there were nineteen cards on it, and he was reading the one with the Halden mark at its head, as though it were a sum that would not come out. He heard her and did not turn. You've heard, he said. Heard what? Then you haven't. He took one hand out of his pocket and touched the card's corner, as Jude had touched his yesterday, and put the hand back. It doesn't matter, it's mine. What do you want at eight in the morning, with your hand in a bandage and that face on? To tell you something before you hear it in a hall tonight, said Kiva, so that you've had it first, from me. He turned round then. She told him on the boards by the draft board, with the timber pond lying black beside them, and the gate mast standing over Noah's empty desk. She did not tell him all of it. She told him that she dreamed with a fever, and had since she was thirteen. It was the thing in Annex notebook, and the Ferran keeper's book, and the keeper's book at the pump house here, on the same night in 2604. Her aunt had written it down the same night last spring, in her words, and had it sealed before she read anybody else's. Kellen listened with his face quite still. When she had done, he did not say anything for a while. He looked at the gate mast. That's not a sum, he said at last. No. I was trying to make it one, while you talked. I can't. He took his hands out of his pockets. I'll tell you what I can do with it. The house will want it. He'll want it more than he wanted the three. Because the three was a thing you could do, and this is a thing you've seen. He's been looking for somebody who saw what he saw, for seventy-seven years. Kellen's voice was flat, as it went when a sum was bad. He'll be glad. That's the part that frightens me. He'll be so glad. Oh no. Do you? He sat at that table and told you about a window. I've heard him tell it four times at dinner. Every time he gets to white, his voice goes quiet. Kellen stopped. I'm not telling you not to. I'd not. I'm telling you what my house will do with it, because nobody else in that hall will know. That's why I told you first, said Kiva. He looked at her. Then he nodded, once, and glanced back at the card on the bays behind him, with the holden mark at its head. Of a thing of my own tonight, he said, in that hall. It's not as big as yours. It's big enough. He did not explain. I'll see you on the floor at eleven. Holden's at nine. I'll be on the tiers for Kero, with the rest of Meridian. Wanting you to lose and wanting you to win. I'd expect nothing else of myself. He went away, toward the graving steps, with his hands back in his pockets. Jude was at the board when Kiva turned round, with the book under his good arm, reading his own card again for the fourth time. He did not mind her reading it over his shoulder. He moved a little to let her. It was a plain white card in the company's green, pinned at the top with one brass pin, in Yow's brisk upright hand. The Saltmere Company. Tally, J. Edge, Meridian, Team 7. To the closing crew under Officer Yow, on the longshore in the boats, at a company hands wage, housed from the first of the fourth month. Six months. And then we look again. A card is not a seat. Yow. Under it, smaller, in the same hand, there was one more line. You asked me on the rope walk steps what it was for. Come and find out. She was at the board on Wednesday night, said Jude. Behind us. She didn't say anything. He looked at the line at the foot. I knew she would. I said so at the window. I said I'd stay if she asked. He scratched his jaw with his right hand. She's asked. I'd thought I'd feel something. I feel as though I've been handed a parcel, and I don't know what's in it, and it's heavy, and it's mine. You don't have to answer today. I know. It says six months, and then we look again. Jude almost smiled. That's Ria's card. She's copied Ria's card. She'll have had it off Rowan's columns, through Ivy. He touched the corner of it again. I'll answer after Wednesday. I want to see the bank come out first. If it comes out. He looked at the sea, past the end of the timber pond and the graving's gate. Grey and breathing. If I'm to spend six months carrying Ash up a bank, I'd like to know first that a bank can be carried down. Perrin's two cards were in the bottom corner, where they had been yesterday. He was standing three paces off, pretending to read the lane board. One cod had the Halden mark. Halden lift yards, the long key, the winner of the carry. Meridian to the lift yard, carry, at a carry's wage, on the proprietor's roll, from his healer's leave. The other was on the works gray paper, in a small square hand. The municipal works, Meridian. Cade, P. Carry, to the trunk crew at the brickfields, from the autumn, when his card is up. Rusk. Two, said a voice behind them. It was Gower, from Old For, with a pasty in his hand, and nothing unkind in his face. Two cards, Cade, for carrying a dummy up a ladder. I carried mine up a stair, and nobody's carded me for anything. You got face, said Perrin. Ten seconds. I got face. I'm not saying I didn't. Gower bit his pasty. I'm saying two. Hesketh's been at the board since seven, counting other people's. Half the loft's been. He went away. Eating. Perrin stood, looking at the two cards with his hand pressed to his side. I wanted it, he said. Kiva did not think he was saying it to her. On the boat. Something with only my name on it. I said so to Price on the rope-walk steps. He reached out with his free hand and took the Holden card down off its pin. That one hasn't got my name on it. It's got the winner of the carry. They've carded a Tuesday. He took a pencil out of his coat and wrote on the back of it, against the bays in his round, careful hand. No, with thanks. It was mine the ladder, but it was one Tuesday. P. Cade. Cade. Then he pinned the card back up, face to the board, so that only the back showed. And the other? It says Cade. He did not touch the grey card. It says when his card is up. Rusk read the chair's ledger and ask's card, both, before he wrote it. That's a man who's counted the ribs. He looked at it for a moment longer. I'll leave it up. I'll answer at home. They went down the graving steps together, slowly, with Perrin a step at a time. Halfway down he stopped and breathed. Gower thinks I'm pleased, he said. Aren't you? I'm pleased about the grey one. He went on down. I'd thought being envied would feel like the top of the ladder. It feels like Gower eating a pasty and counting. He was quiet for three steps. Give me the foot of the ladder and you saying set. The graving was full at a quarter to eleven, and the whole of it was green. Kiva had thought it was full a week ago, on the Saturday, against the Tarn's first four. She had been wrong. That Saturday, there had been room on the tiers to put a hand down beside you. Now, the green came down the steps to the floor's edge and stood there, ten deep on the bottom tier, and the boys who sold pasties had given up selling and were sitting on their baskets. The brown and buff of the Tarn sat in its knot in the middle. Meridian's colours were above it, all four of the first company, and Kellan among them in his black and gold. The iron and glass roof went over all of it, and the grey light came down on the white chalk of the pen eighty feet below, as it comes down into a church. At the seaward end, the floating gate held the harbour out, and Kiva could hear the sea breathing against its timber. Under that, through the stone of the dock floor, there was the town's count. The rope walk's first four came out of the side door in their shirt sleeves, and the graving stood up. It did not cheer. It stood, all of it, tier after tier, as a church stands. Caro walked first, with the rope on her sleeve. Lyle walked half a pace behind and to one side, as she always had. But there was nothing at her hip now, and her hands hung at her sides. Tolver came after, with his cheerful face. Treen came last, small and dark, with her sleeves rolled and her cord at her belt. They stood behind their hurdle and looked at the Commodore lying in the middle of the pen. Then Caro looked down the pen, at Seven. She looked at Perrin outside the pen, behind Seven's hurdle, with his hand on his side. She looked at Jude's left arm, and Prue's ten caps, two of them fresh, and the linen on Kiva's right hand. She looked at them each for exactly as long as it took to see what was there. And then she looked at Kiva and inclined her head, as a fact about the weather. The rope walk, said Caro. Her voice went up the stone walls, low and flat and pleasant, with the coast in it. Caro, edge, declared, single. The graving made a sound. It was very small. It was the sound of four thousand people drawing in their breath and not letting it out. Loyal, stance. Single. Tulvor, stance. Treen, ward. At the mast on the north side of the pen, Noah wrote. Polglace wrote. Kiva saw Noah look up at Caro from his desk, once with his narrow face quite still, and then down again. Time Seven, said Perrin. Price, ward. Tally, edge. Finch, ward, catcher. Rowan, stance, declared. By her captain's voice. Kate, captain, standing out on his healer's card. One door each, said the marshal, to nobody in particular, and then looked as though he wished he had not. He turned his glass. Ready? They had made the plan at the long table at half past nine, and it was Thursday's plan, because Thursday's plan had worked. Kiva would plant on the litter's head and sit there, as she had sat on it against the tarn, so that nobody could carry what nobody could lift. Anwen's wall would keep their still doors off the foot. Jude would take whoever came near, with his edge on his right fist. Prue would call hands. And at the glass, the point was sevens, every carry, and whatever Jude cut. And in the third carry, if it was close, they would try the hurdle with their elbows. Caro had been on the tiers on Thursday afternoon. Kiva had seen her, two rows below Rhea, with Trine beside her, watching. The bell went. Kiva went for the litter. She got there first. She went down astride the head poles, with her forearms along the canvas, and opened her stance. And her feet went into the graving's floor, down through the granite, and held. Anwen's wall came up on the south side of the foot. Jude went north. Prue stood behind the litter's middle, with her ward at her hip. Low, and her eyes on hands. Lyle walked down the pen, and stopped, two paces from Anwen's wall, and planted. She did not have a wall. She had nothing at her hip, and nothing on her hands. She stood with her feet in the stone, and her arms at her sides. And then she bent her knees, and put her weight down into the floor, and leaned her shoulder against Anwen's wall. Kiva saw Anwen feel it. She saw Anwen's heels go into the stone, right, and her wall bow, a finger, two fingers. Lyle was leaning from the floor. She was leaning as Anwen had taught her to lean on a bare board at eight o'clock yesterday morning, with her weight going down and coming back up through her heels and her back and her shoulder, and it was moving Anwen's wall. She's got it, said Anwen, between her teeth. I gave it her. Karo had not moved from the rope walk's end of the pen. She stood a pace behind Treen, with her edge lit on her right fist, bright as a poker, and her feet on the stone like anybody's. And she was not looking at the litter at all. She was looking at nothing. Treen was looking at Jude. Set, said Treen. Karo walked. It was not a run. She walked down the south side of the pen, past the chalk squares, toward the litter, with her edge lit, and her feet coming up off the stone at every step. Kiva felt it go past her through the floor, loud, as Lyle had said it would be loud. It was one door, walking. Jude went to meet her. That was the plan. Whoever came near, Jude took them. Hans north, said Prue. Jude checked. Tolva had come up on the north side, very fast for a big boy, with his long arms out and his still door ready, reaching for the litter's head poles, where they stuck out past Kiva's forearms. Jude turned to take him. It was the right thing to do. Prue had called it. And it was right. Set, said Treen. Karo was apace from the litter. Her edge came down on the word, flat, quite lightly, on Kiva's shoulder. Down, said the marshal. Seven. Kiva knelt. Kiva knelt. She had to shut and let go to Neil. And the moment she let go of the poles, Tolva had them. He did not lift. He held the head. And Lyle came off Anwen's wall. And the two still doors took the Commodore by the poles together. And walked him back down the pen, as two men carry a sleeping friend upstairs. Karo walked beside them, with her edge lit. Jude went for Tolva's back, and Treen said hands. And Karo's edge came round between them. And Jude stopped, because the alternative was to walk into it. At the rope walk's hurdle, Karo shut, and vaulted the hazel, and turned. And took the head poles from under on the far side. Treen came over after her and took the foot. Three, said the marshal, and down. Four. To the rope walk. Begraving did not make the warm sound. It let its breath out. It was a long sound, like a wave going back off shingle. And it went round the tears and came back. And then the green began to talk. All at once. Kiva knelt on the stone in the middle of the pen, with her hands on her knees, and counted ten, as a downed fighter counts. And did not look at anybody. She had seen it. She had seen it from her knees, a pace off, with her shoulder still warm where the edge had touched. Karo had not looked at the litter. She had not looked at Jude. She had walked down the pen with her eyes on nothing, and her edge lit. And she had brought it down when Treen spoke, and not a hair before. Treen had been watching Jude's hands. When Jude's hands went north, Treen said, set. She was not reading the lane. She was being read for. She's taking Treen's count, said Kiva, at the hurdle, in the pause. Perrin was outside the pen, with his hands on the hazel, not leaning. Anwen was white and breathing hard, with her forearm shaking in her sleeves. Jude had his edge shut, and his right fist opening and closing at his side. She's never done that, said Kiva. Not in the rope walk, not at the hunt. Karo reads everything herself. That's what she is. She heard her voice go flat, and let it. Now she doesn't read anything. She walks, and Treen reads. And Treen says, set, and she brings it down. It's what I did to you on the ladder. Set, off your heel. She's had it off you, said Anwen. On the inner lock, half the town was on the lip. She's had it off me, said Kiva. And it works. She's not got two doors to lay, so she's got two people instead. Treen's eyes and her edge. So we take Treen's eyes, said Jude. How, said Perrin. Kiva had been asking herself that on her knees for a count of ten. She looked at Prue. Prue had her hands up in front of her face, in their caps. She was looking at them. At the linen on the tips of her fingers. Two of them fresh. And then at Kiva's right hand, in its bandage. And then at Jude's left arm hanging. Train watches hands, said Prue slowly. Like me. She's a hand door. She watches hands because she is one. She looked up. That's what you said to me, on the steps, after the tarn. Yes. Five hundred and siftin' faust. She went scarlet all the way up. She'll have to read something else. And she's never had to. And by the time she's found it, we're at the hurdle. Perrin made a sound that was not quite a laugh. He took his hands off the hazel. No sitting on it, he said. Not against a blade who's being read for. We carry. On your arms. Finch and Rowan on the poles. Elbows. All the way down the pen. And Price and Tali off them. He looked at Anwen. Lyle's leaning on you with your own lean. I know she is. Then don't lean back. Walk. Perrin's face was the colour it went when he was thinking very hard. Walk your wall from the far end. Round her. The way you'd walk it round a post. She's planted. She can lean, but she can't follow. Rowan. Rowan. Said the marshal. Your declaration for the second carry. Ember. Said Perrin. Before Kiva could open her mouth. Rowan. Ember. Declared. Single. By her captain's voice. He did not look at her. You'll not need your stance if you're not sitting on it. You'll need your legs. A change between carries. Said the marshal. Declared to the box. With nothing open in the paws. It's on her cart. At the mast. Noah wrote. The second carry was the best four minutes of lane Kiva had ever stood in. And she could not afterward remember more than half of it. She remembered the bell. She remembered going for the litters head with her ember lit under her breastbone. Glad as it always came. And the low bound it gave her down the stone. She remembered putting her forearms under the head poles. Both of them. The left sleeve and the right bandage. Crossed at the wrists as one holds out one's arms for a coat. She remembered the weight coming down into the crooks of her elbows. And Prue beside her at the foot. With her forearms crooked. And her capped fingers spread up and out. Like the fingers of a girl drying her nails. She remembered that her hands were in the air. And so were Prue's. And that there was nothing on the poles but cloth and bone. And she remembered Trine. Trine was at the ropewalk's end. With her ward low at her hip. And her eyes going quick and dark. From Kiva's arms to Prue's. From Prue's to Jude's fist and back. Kiva saw her look for hands and not find them. She saw Trine's mouth open on a word and shut again. Caro was walking down the south side of the pen. With her edge lit. Waiting to be told. As two washerwomen walk a basket between them. Behind them, Anwen had stopped leaning. Lyle was planted two paces off her wall. With her shoulder against it. Leaning from the floor. Anwen walked the far end of her wall round. She did not push the near end. She walked the far end in a quarter circle. Slowly. As Mace had taught her on a van's line at home. And the near end came after it. Lyle leaned on a wall. Lyle leaned on a wall. That was no longer where she was leaning. She leaned on air from the floor. With her feet planted and all her weight coming up through her heels. And there was nothing there. She did not fall. She was too good to fall. But she had to shut her stance to keep her feet. And for a count she stood in the middle of the pen with nothing open at all. And Jude was there. Down, said the marshal. The rope walk. Lyle knelt. Kiva saw her face as she went down. Square and careful. Filing a thing away to be thought about later. Then she saw Lyle look across the pen at Anwen and, for the first time Kiva had ever seen, nearly smile. Set, said Trine. It was late. Kiva heard that it was late. Trine had found something to read at last. Jude's feet. Coming back from Lyle. Wide and slow on the bad side. She said, set off his feet. And Caro brought her edge down where Jude was going to be. Jude was not there. He had stopped. He had stopped because he had heard Prue say, quite quietly, tally, stay. And he stayed. A pace short. It was not the warm sound, and it was not the long sound of breath going out. It was somebody high up, a long way off, shouting elbows, in a voice that cracked, and then a great many people laughing, and some of them were in green. They lost the third carry by the glass, and it was Kiva's fault, and Prue's, and nobody's. The rope walk had learned. Kiva watched Trine learn it in the pause, at the far hurdle, with Caro bent beside her, and the two of them talking very fast and low. When the bell went, Trine did not look for hands. She looked at feet. She had watched Jude's feet in the second carry, and found she could read them, and now she was reading everybody's. Anwen's heels, Prue's quick small steps, Kiva's own boots coming down after the embers bound. She had taken that off Kiva too. Kiva watched feet. Everybody on the circuit knew it. Pike had said it on a tailboard in front of Half Greywater. You watch where people put their feet. It was a strange thing to see your own habit in somebody else's eyes, being used against you. I'd like you to say it, said Kiva, under your own name, the held slack, the dog, that on Wednesday it'll not walk, and nobody can say why, and you've written it every spring since the ninth month. She made herself go on. I'm asking a thing of a ruined hand, I know I am. I don't know what you'll let ask it. He looked at her for a long time from the landing, with the brown water still and flat below him, and the six outfalls pouring into it on the count, and the count not going anywhere. It's let be asked one thing, he said at last, quiet or not. That's all it does. It doesn't know why or what or how long. It knows quiet. He turned his bad hand over on the rail, palm up, as Lyle had held her hand at her hip with nothing in it. It was the best hand at the bench in 2660, your sponsor will tell you. It could read a cell through a wall. Now it reads one thing and aches near everything else, and a girl from Meridian with two dead fingers has come down a walk to ask it to stand up in a hall. He was quiet a moment. Nobody's asked anything of it in 20 years. But is it quiet yet, Jess? I'm asking. I heard you. He shut his book of slacks. Your sponsor will be in that hall. Yes. Then so will I. He put the book in his jacket. I'll say what the hand says and I'll say it's ruined before anybody else does, and then I'll sit down. He looked at her. You've not come here to ask me that. That's the second thing. What's the first? She had not known it showed. She stood on the walk and found that it did, and that she did not mind it showing to him. I'm going to stand up as well, she said, after Mara, about a thing that isn't a door. Hart did not ask what. She had thought he might. He looked at her face for a long time, and at her hands, and then he turned his watch on his wrist, once, and looked at the water. Aichi, he said quietly. Thirty-nine past. That's twenty minutes. It's going out again. He did not look round. Same hour every day, Rowan. Never on purpose. You'll have done it already today. Not yet. A quarter to seven. Then you'll be in a hall at a quarter to seven, standing up. Lay them on the rail of the salt hall's gallery. It's iron. It'll say yes. Everything in this town says yes. Write it down anyway.
